analysis|11-20|1989|Ξεκινά το Mega Channel|Mega Channel begins|At the end of the 1980s the state monopoly over television had begun to collapse, with private stations operating and seeking legal cover. Mega was the first channel with nationwide reach and was founded by businessmen from the publishing sector. Its business base gave the station strong organisation. // Its appearance created competition for audiences and for advertising. New types of programmes, game shows and series were established, and the news bulletins acquired a major role in public debate. // Television became a powerful factor in Greek society and politics. Mega remains in history as one of the pioneers of private television in the country.

analysis|11-21|1916|Βυθίζεται το «Βρετανικός» στην Κέα|The Britannic sinks off Kea|The Britannic was built as an ocean liner, but in the First World War it was converted into a hospital ship for the wounded of the Mediterranean campaign. On 21 November 1916 it suffered an explosion in the strait of Kea and sank within about an hour. The incident was tragic for the war effort of the Allies. // Most of those on board were saved, although there were losses. Violet Jessop, who had survived the collision of the Olympic and the sinking of the Titanic, was once again on the ship. // The wreck, one of the largest on the seabed, is a notable naval and historical monument. The ship's story links the Greek sea with the history of the First World War.

analysis|11-22|1897|Συνθήκη ειρήνης μετά τον πόλεμο του 1897|Peace treaty after the war of 1897|The war of 1897, known as the Unlucky War, broke out after the Cretan crisis and Greece's pressure for the union of Crete. The Greek army was defeated in Thessaly by the Ottoman forces, and the Great Powers intervened to stop the war. The short duration of the clash reflected the imbalance of forces. // The peace was signed in Constantinople, and the Greek budget was burdened with a war indemnity and an international financial control. Minor border adjustments in Thessaly in favour of the Ottomans were also necessary. // The war subsequently led to reforms in the army after 1909. The defeat of 1897 remained in memory as a lesson for the organisation of the armed forces.

analysis|11-22|1940|Ο ελληνικός στρατός μπαίνει στην Κορυτσά|The Greek army enters Korytsa|After the Italian invasion of 28 October 1940 and its repulsion, the Greek army passed to the counter-offensive and advanced onto Albanian territory. Korytsa was a large city in south-eastern Albania, with important roads and significance for the military situation. This advance was unexpected for the opponents. // Its capture was an important victory, because it showed that the Greek army could defeat Axis forces. It strengthened morale in Greece and in countries fighting the Axis. // The Greek forces remained in the area until the German invasion of April 1941. This period remained in memory as one of the most brilliant moments of the Greco-Italian War.

analysis|11-23|1988|Συλλαμβάνεται ο Γιώργος Κοσκωτάς|Giorgos Koskotas is arrested|Giorgos Koskotas was head of the Bank of Crete, and in 1988 he was accused of embezzling large sums. The scandal was linked with politicians and caused intense political turmoil. His arrest in the United States took place at the end of 1988. // The affair shook the government of Andreas Papandreou and contributed to the electoral defeat of PASOK in 1989. The public argument about responsibility was intense. // A trial of former ministers followed before the Special Court, something rare for the country, and the scandal became a landmark in the discussion about transparency and the accountability of politicians. The case remains as one of the best-known instances of political accountability in the country.

analysis|11-23|1989|Οικουμενική κυβέρνηση του Ζολώτα|The all-party government of Zolotas|The elections of June 1989 did not give a clear majority, and a second election in November continued the deadlock. With the climate of the Koskotas scandal weighing heavily, the three parties agreed on an all-party government. That agreement was unprecedented in Greek politics. // Xenophon Zolotas, a former governor of the Bank of Greece, was appointed head. His choice gave the government a technocratic character. // Its role was to lead to the elections of 1990 and to calm the political climate. The government was temporary but important, since it showed that the parties could cooperate in periods of crisis.

analysis|11-24|1826|Ο Καραϊσκάκης νικά στην Αράχωβα|Karaiskakis wins at Arachova|After the long siege and the sortie from Missolonghi, Central Greece was exposed. Georgios Karaiskakis had taken on the defence of the area and was trying to stop the Ottoman and Albanian forces that wanted to take Arachova. His position was difficult and vital. // The victory came in the middle of winter and had great moral significance for the Struggle at a difficult moment. This success strengthened the cohesion of the fighters of Central Greece. // Karaiskakis became even better known, and his name was linked with the battles of Central Greece before his death in 1827. His figure remains as a symbol of the heroism of the Revolution.

analysis|11-24|1912|Απελευθερώνεται η Χίος|Chios is liberated|Chios was one of the Aegean islands that remained under Ottoman rule after the foundation of the Greek state, and the destruction of 1822 had left deep wounds in the memory of its inhabitants. In the First Balkan War the Greek navy took action in the islands of the eastern Aegean. The prospect of liberation was greatly anticipated. // The liberation of Chios incorporated the island into the Greek state, something that was confirmed internationally in 1913. This change completed a long wait of the inhabitants. // The event was part of the wider expansion of Greece and satisfied the desire of the island population for union. The incorporation of Chios remained in memory as one of the high points of the Balkan War.

analysis|11-25|1916|Αποκλεισμός της Ελλάδας από την Αντάντ|Allied blockade of Greece|In the First World War Greece was divided between King Konstantinos, who wanted neutrality, and Venizelos, who called for entry into the war on the side of the Entente. Venizelos had formed a rival government in Thessaloniki. That clash was the centre of the National Schism. // The Entente, to pressure the government in Athens, imposed a blockade that caused shortages and difficulties for the population. The blockade became a pressing means of forcing a change of policy. // The blockade intensified the National Schism and led in 1917 to the abdication of Konstantinos and to the country's entry into the war. This development changed the course of the Greek state.

analysis|11-25|1935|Ο Γεώργιος Β΄ επιστρέφει|George II returns|George II had left Greece in 1923, when the country was in crisis after the Asia Minor catastrophe, and in 1924 the Hellenic Republic was proclaimed. After the coup of 1935 and the abolition of the constitutional system, a referendum gave an overwhelming majority in favour of his return. The return took place in a climate of intense political polarisation. // The king went back to Athens and the monarchy was restored. This return changed the balance of forces in the political scene. // In 1936 he supported the dictatorship of Ioannis Metaxas, and this stance marked his political course and the discussion about the role of the throne. The historical question of the king's role remains open.

analysis|11-25|1942|Ανατινάζεται η γέφυρα του Γοργοπόταμου|The Gorgopotamos bridge is blown up|After the occupation of Greece by the Axis, the resistance was organised into various groups. The railway line that passed over the Gorgopotamos bridge carried supplies to Rommel's army in North Africa. The line was of strategic importance to the Axis. // Guerrillas of EDES and ELAS, together with British saboteurs, blew up the bridge. It was the largest act of sabotage in occupied Europe, and it had military as well as psychological value. The cooperation of the groups was rare at that time. // It encouraged the resistance and showed that the resistance fighters could cooperate with the Allies. The operation remains as a milestone in the history of the National Resistance.

analysis|11-26|1955|Κήρυξη κατάστασης έκτακτης ανάγκης|Declaration of a state of emergency|EOKA had begun its armed struggle for the union of Cyprus with Greece on 1 April 1955. The British governor John Harding, a field marshal who had recently taken up the post, announced a state of emergency in November. The announcement was a response to the escalation of violence. // The measures included arrests, restrictions of freedoms and harsher repression. These methods affected the daily life of Cypriots. // They did not stop the struggle, but made it harsher, and the relations of the Cypriots with the British administration deteriorated. This situation lasted until independence.

analysis|11-26|1963|Ξεκινά η δωρεάν παιδεία|Free education begins|The idea of free education had a long history in Greece, as tuition fees at the universities made it difficult for the poorer strata to study. Within the framework of the political change of 1963 and of the educational reforms, enrolment without fees was an important step. The measure reflected social demands. // The reform widened access to higher education and later became a basic principle of Greek education. The social dimension of the measure was evident in the years that followed. // Today the Constitution provides that education in state institutions is free. This principle is connected with the idea of equal access to knowledge.

analysis|11-27|1919|Η συνθήκη του Νεϊγύ|The Treaty of Neuilly|Bulgaria had fought alongside the Central Powers in the First World War and was defeated. The Treaty of Neuilly, near Paris, set the terms of peace, with territorial losses, reparations and military restrictions. This treaty was part of the settlement that followed the war. // Bulgaria lost its outlet to the Aegean, and Western Thrace was placed under Allied control. That loss closed the question of Bulgaria's access to the sea. // In 1920 the area was given to Greece, with the Treaty of Sèvres and the San Remo agreement. The event completed the Greek presence in eastern Macedonia and in Thrace.

analysis|11-28|1910|Ο Βενιζέλος κερδίζει τις δεύτερες εκλογές του έτους|Venizelos wins the second elections of the year|Eleftherios Venizelos came from Crete and took over the premiership in 1910, after the Goudi coup of 1909. Parliament was dissolved and elections were held in August, and then again in November, after the revisionary Parliament. The old parties withdrew from the contest. This situation gave Venizelos broad political power. // The Liberal Party won an overwhelming majority and brought reforms to the administration, the army and the economy. The victory gave the government a mandate for sweeping changes. // This period prepared Greece for the Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913. The reforms of that era are regarded as fundamental to the military readiness of the country.

analysis|11-28|1925|Παύονται ο Γληνός και ο Δελμούζος|Glinos and Delmouzos are dismissed|Alexandros Delmouzos and Miltiadis Glinos were educators who supported the demotic language and a more modern education at the Marasli Teacher Training College for Women. Their ideas brought them into conflict with conservative circles that defended the katharevousa. The dispute concerned the very nature of education. // Their dismissal from their posts became a landmark in the language question. The decision provoked strong reactions in educational circles. // The question of the language of education remained open for decades, until the law of 1976 established the demotic in schools, and later the reform of the language was completed. This development was linked with the ideas of the two educators.

analysis|11-30|1963|Τα δεκατρία σημεία του Μακαρίου|Makarios' thirteen points|The Republic of Cyprus had been founded in 1960, but the Constitution, which rested on the agreements of Zurich and London, created deadlocks in the functioning of the state. President Makarios proposed thirteen points of revision to make it more workable. The proposal was the answer to practical problems of the system. // The Turkish Cypriot side and Turkey rejected them, and a few weeks later the incidents of December 1963 broke out. The rejection became the occasion for an escalation of tension. // The proposal remains a subject of debate as to whether it was a reasonable attempt at structural change or a pretext for escalation. The historical verdict on the proposal has not been definitively closed.

analysis|11-30|2024|Εγκαινιάζεται το Μετρό Θεσσαλονίκης|The Thessaloniki Metro is inaugurated|Thessaloniki had discussed for decades the construction of a metro, in order to address traffic congestion. The works were delayed for a long time, mainly because important antiquities were found during the excavations, especially at Venizelou station. That discovery forced changes to the plan. // The first line opened to the public in 2024 and is the largest transport project in the city. Its operation changed the way residents travel. // The preservation of the antiquities within the stations gives additional cultural interest, and the metro is expected to change the movements and the image of the city. The connection of the project with antiquity became one of its characteristic features.

analysis|12-01|1818|Ο Κολοκοτρώνης μυείται στη Φιλική Εταιρεία|Kolokotronis is initiated into the Philiki Etaireia|The Philiki Etaireia was founded in Odessa in 1814 with the aim of preparing the national uprising. It needed military leaders with authority and experience, and Theodoros Kolokotronis, who had served in the Ionian Islands, was a natural choice. The need was pressing in the preparation of the struggle. // His initiation strengthened the organisation in the Peloponnese and gave the Philiki Members a significant support. His presence in the circle of the Etaireia gave the struggle a real military dimension. // In 1821 he became one of the main military leaders of the Revolution and linked his name with the victory at Dervenakia and the capture of Tripolitsa. This course made Kolokotronis one of the best-known figures of the Struggle.

analysis|12-01|1913|Η Κρήτη ενώνεται με την Ελλάδα|Crete is united with Greece|Crete had been under Ottoman rule for more than two centuries, and the Cretans had carried out many revolutions, among them those of 1821, 1866 and 1897. After the war of 1897 the Great Powers imposed the Cretan State, an autonomous regime under the nominal suzerainty of the Sultan, with Prince George of Greece as High Commissioner. The question of union, however, remained open, and the revolt of Therisso in 1905, led by Eleftherios Venizelos, increased the popular demand. // In the First Balkan War of 1912 Greece was victorious, and Crete declared that it regarded itself as part of the Greek state. The Treaty of London of May 1913 placed the island at the disposal of the allied Balkan states, and in effect at Greece's. The official ceremony took place at Chania on 1 December 1913 (18 November by the old calendar), with the raising of the Greek flag over the Firka fortress in the presence of King Konstantinos and Venizelos. // The union completed a struggle of decades and strengthened the prestige of Greece after the Balkan Wars. For the Cretans it was the fulfilment of a longing at a heavy price in sacrifice. Crete thenceforth became an inseparable part of the state, and Venizelos, who had been born on the island, became a central figure of Greek politics.

analysis|12-01|1913|Υψώνεται η ελληνική σημαία στα Χανιά|The Greek flag is raised in Chania|The union of Crete with Greece was the result of many decades of struggle. From the Revolution of 1821 to the uprisings of 1866 and 1897, the Cretans demanded union, while the Great Powers hesitated because of the balances in the region. The Cretan State (1898-1913) was an interim solution that did not fully satisfy the population. // Greece's victories in the Balkan Wars changed the situation, and by the Treaty of London in 1913 the Ottoman Empire renounced its rights over the island. The ceremony of the formal union took place at the Firka fortress of Chania, with the lowering of the Cretan flag and the raising of the Greek flag by King Konstantinos, in the presence of Prime Minister Eleftherios Venizelos. The people celebrated with emotion, because the longing for union had become reality. // The raising of the flag became a symbol of the Cretan struggle for freedom, and 1 December is celebrated to this day in Chania. The event closed a page in the history of Crete and fully integrated it into the Greek state, at a time when the country was almost doubling its territory.

analysis|12-02|1979|Ο Γκάλης στον Άρη|Galis at Aris|At the end of the 1970s basketball in Greece was popular but did not yet have the reach it later acquired. Nikos Galis was born in the United States to Greek parents, grew up in New Jersey and played university basketball, and came to Greece with the support of his Greek origins. Aris Thessaloniki took him on, and the club already had a team with ambitions. // On his debut Galis scored 30 points, which gave a great warning of what was to follow. Over the years he became the leading player of the championship, with impressive ability in scoring and in play, and together with Panagiotis Giannakis and others led his team into a golden era. // His presence changed the image of Greek basketball. With the national team he won the 1987 EuroBasket in Athens, and the sporting public filled the arenas. That success is regarded as a landmark and gave impetus to the spread of the sport in the country.

analysis|12-03|1944|Αρχίζουν τα Δεκεμβριανά|The Dekemvriana begin|After the withdrawal of the German forces in October 1944, Greece found itself in deep political division. The government of Papandreou, which had returned from the Middle East with British support, sought the disarmament of the guerrilla groups, while EAM feared it would lose its political power. The ministers of EAM resigned and called a mass rally. // On 3 December the police fired on demonstrators, and Athens found itself in civil war. ELAS took control of much of the city, while the British, led by General Scobie and with strong support from Churchill, were reinforced with troops. The battles lasted until about January 1945, with many casualties and great destruction. // The end came with a truce and the Agreement of Varkiza. The Dekemvriana further divided Greek society, left bitter memories and became one of the main events in the prehistory of the Civil War. The discussion of responsibility continues to this day.

analysis|12-05|1912|Η πρώτη αναγνωριστική πτήση|The first reconnaissance flight|The First Balkan War of 1912 was one of the first wars in which aircraft were used, and Greece, which had shortly before founded its first military aviation service with a few aircraft and Greek officers trained abroad, wanted to acquire this new capability. Lieutenant Michail Moutousis was among the first Greek pilots. // The reconnaissance flight over Ottoman positions gave the Greek army information about the movements of the enemy. Such flights were then pioneering, dangerous and technically limited, since the aircraft were fragile and the equipment very simple. The event showed the usefulness of aviation for observing the battlefield. // That experience was the beginning of the Greek military air force. Over the following decades the branch developed into an independent force, and the first pilots are regarded as pioneers of the Greek air force.

analysis|12-05|1920|Το δημοψήφισμα για την επιστροφή του Κωνσταντίνου|The referendum on the return of Konstantinos|King Konstantinos I had been forced to leave the country in 1917 during the National Schism, and his son Alexandros had ascended the throne. Alexandros died in October 1920 from a monkey bite, and the question of succession came to the fore. A few weeks earlier the government of Eleftherios Venizelos had lost the November elections to the opposition, which demanded the return of Konstantinos. // The referendum of 5 December 1920 gave an overwhelming majority in favour of the return, although the conditions and the credibility of the process have been debated, since the form of state was not under question and the process was polarised. // The return of Konstantinos brought a change in alliances, as the Allies, and in particular France and Britain, had a negative stance towards him. Greece continued the military campaign in Asia Minor with less international support, and this course ultimately led to the Asia Minor Catastrophe of 1922 and to a new political crisis.

analysis|12-06|1940|Ο ελληνικός στρατός μπαίνει στους Αγίους Σαράντα|The Greek army enters Agioi Saranta|After the Italian invasion of October 1940 and the repulsion of the attackers in Epirus, the Greek army passed to the counter-offensive and advanced onto Albanian territory. Korytsa had been taken at the end of November, and the Greek forces continued towards the southern part of Albania, despite the difficult winter and the mountainous terrain. // In early December the army reached and captured Agioi Saranta, a town on the Albanian coast opposite Corfu, with a considerable population of Greek origin. It was one of the most important successes of the campaign, which raised morale and strengthened Greece's standing in international public opinion. // The advance subsequently halted because of bad weather, supply difficulties and Italian resistance. The front stabilised during the winter of 1941, until the German invasion of April changed the situation. Even so, the Albanian campaign remained in memory as one of the most glorious episodes of modern Greek history.

analysis|12-06|2008|Δολοφονία του Αλέξανδρου Γρηγορόπουλου|Murder of Alexandros Grigoropoulos|On the evening of Saturday 6 December 2008, in Exarcheia in Athens, a fifteen-year-old schoolboy, Alexandros Grigoropoulos, was killed by a policeman's bullet after a verbal altercation between a group of young people and two special guards. Greek society was already in a climate of tension, with economic insecurity and distrust of institutions. // The news spread instantly and provoked demonstrations and riots, first in Athens and then in other cities. Pupils and students took part to a large extent, with school occupations and gatherings, while there were damage and clashes with the police. The policeman who fired was later convicted by the courts. // The events of December 2008 became a point of reference for the youth and for its relationship with the state. The police violence, unemployment and disappointment of young people were discussed, and many see in the uprising an early image of the crisis that followed in 2010. The anniversary continues to be marked by marches.

analysis|12-07|1974|Ο Μακάριος επιστρέφει στην Κύπρο|Makarios returns to Cyprus|On 15 July 1974 the military junta in Athens organised a coup against President Makarios through the National Guard, and Makarios escaped from Paphos with British help. A few days later Turkey invaded Cyprus, occupying the northern part, and the junta in Greece collapsed. Makarios found himself abroad, seeking international support. // After months of absence the Archbishop returned to Nicosia on 7 December 1974 and was welcomed by a large crowd. He was once again the recognised president of the Republic of Cyprus, and he continued the struggle for the recovery of territories and the return of refugees. // His return was a powerful symbolic event for a people that had suffered trauma, displacement and division. Makarios remained president until his death in 1977, and his policy between union and independence remains a subject of debate in the history of the island.

analysis|12-07|2008|Οι ταραχές μετά τον θάνατο του Αλέξανδρου Γρηγορόπουλου|The riots after the death of Alexandros Grigoropoulos|The death of the fifteen-year-old Alexandros Grigoropoulos in Exarcheia on the evening of 6 December 2008 was the spark for a wave of anger. Greek society already had several causes of discontent: youth unemployment, economic uncertainty, scandals and clashes with the police from earlier incidents. // On the next day, 7 December, the demonstrations and riots spread to several cities in the country, such as Thessaloniki, Patras and Heraklion. Damage was caused to shops and public buildings, there were clashes with the police and use of tear gas, while pupils occupied schools and held gatherings. The situation lasted several weeks. // The developments affected political life and the government of the time, and raised questions about youth, police violence and public trust. In historical assessment, this uprising is regarded as one of the most important social events of the Metapolitefsi and is linked with the economic crisis that was approaching.

analysis|12-08|1966|Το ναυάγιο του «Ηράκλειον»|The sinking of the Iraklion|The passenger and car ferry Iraklion operated routes from Crete to Piraeus. It was an old ship that had been converted, and during its journey at night it encountered severe rough seas and problems with its cargo and stability, in an area south of Falconara. // The ship sank in the Aegean and more than two hundred people lost their lives, with only a few survivors. It was the greatest maritime tragedy of Greece in peacetime and caused grief across the country, especially in Crete, where many relatives mourned. // The inquiry that followed brought to light problems in the safety of the ship and in the control of passenger vessels, and led to stricter regulations. The wreck remains in collective memory as a reminder of the need for safety at sea, and above all of the value of every human life.

analysis|12-08|1971|Το πρώτο bypass στην Ελλάδα|The first bypass in Greece|Heart disease was among the main causes of death in the 20th century, and cardiac surgery made great progress in the 1960s and 1970s. The coronary artery bypass graft, known as bypass, was developed internationally at that time and gave new therapeutic possibilities to patients with narrowing of the coronary arteries. // The cardiac surgeon Georgios Tolis performed the first such operation in Greece, at the Evangelismos hospital in Athens. The operation required specialised staff, equipment and experience, and signalled that the country could follow developments in international medicine. // In the following years these operations became more frequent and helped save many patients. Cardiac surgery in Greece developed with the creation of specialised centres, and the first operation is regarded as a milestone in the history of Greek medicine.

analysis|12-08|1974|Το δημοψήφισμα για το πολίτευμα|The referendum on the form of state|After the fall of the dictatorship in July 1974, the government of Konstantinos Karamanlis promised to resolve definitively the question of the form of state, which had troubled the country since the early 20th century. King Konstantinos II had left for abroad after the failed coup of 1967, and the junta had abolished the monarchy in 1973. // On 8 December 1974 citizens were called to choose between a crowned and a republican form of state. About 69% voted for the republic, and the institution of the monarchy was abolished definitively. Konstantinos did not return, and the country proceeded to shape a new Constitution. // The result closed a long period of political division around the role of the throne and gave the Metapolitefsi a more stable basis. The Constitution of 1975 established a parliamentary republic with a presidential element, and the question of the form of state no longer occupied public life intensely.

analysis|12-09|2002|Το αναθεωρημένο σχέδιο Ανάν|The revised Annan plan|The Cyprus issue had remained unresolved since the Turkish invasion of 1974 and the division of the island. In the early 2000s Cyprus was moving towards accession to the European Union, and the UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan attempted to propose a comprehensive plan that would reunite the island before accession. The first text was presented in November 2002 and provoked reactions and comments. // The revised plan, handed to the two sides in December, provided for a federal United Cyprus Republic with two constituent states, and arrangements for territory, property, security and governance. The two leaderships had different approaches, and negotiations continued with the deadlines of the Copenhagen Summit pressing. // The plan reached its final form in 2004 and was put to a referendum, in which Greek Cypriots rejected it and Turkish Cypriots approved it. Cyprus joined the European Union as a divided island. The Annan plan remains a point of reference for every discussion on a solution.

analysis|12-10|1893|«Δυστυχώς επτωχεύσαμεν»|Unfortunately we have gone bankrupt|In the 1880s Greece, under the leadership of Charilaos Trikoupis, borrowed large sums from abroad to build roads, railways, harbours and the Corinth Canal. The economy, however, rested on currants, the main export product, and the crisis in the currant trade, together with the high costs of the army, led to deficits. // In 1893 Trikoupis announced to Parliament that the state could not service all of its debt, with the phrase Unfortunately we have gone bankrupt. The creditors reacted and the country came into conflict with the markets. Trikoupis lost the elections of 1895, while the country found itself in a difficult position. // After the war of 1897 an International Financial Commission was imposed to collect part of the revenues. The bankruptcy of 1893 is regarded as a critical event of economic history, and the phrase is often cited in the modern debate on public debt.

analysis|12-11|969|Δολοφονείται ο αυτοκράτορας Νικηφόρος Β΄ Φωκάς|Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas is murdered|Nikephoros Phokas was one of the most capable generals of Byzantium and ascended the throne in 963, married to the widow of the previous emperor. He had recaptured Crete from the Arabs in 961, and later Cyprus and parts of Cilicia and Syria. The campaigns, however, required high taxes and provoked discontent. // Nikephoros lost his popularity in the capital, and his conflict with the Church and with sections of the aristocracy left him in a weak position. On 11 December 969 conspirators led by his nephew John Tzimiskes entered the palace and killed him. The Empress Theophano is said to have taken part in the conspiracy. // Tzimiskes took the throne and continued the Byzantine victories in the East and in the Balkans. The murder showed the fragility of power in Byzantium, but also how a successful military policy could be continued by its successors.

analysis|12-12|1452|Η ένωση των Εκκλησιών στην Αγία Σοφία|The union of the Churches at Hagia Sophia|Byzantium was threatened by the Ottomans, and the emperors sought military help from the West. In exchange, the Catholic Church demanded the union of the Churches, which had been agreed at the Council of Ferrara-Florence in 1439. In Constantinople, however, many clerics and believers opposed the union, which they regarded as a retreat. // On 12 December 1452, a few months before the Fall, Cardinal Isidore, the papal envoy, celebrated a liturgy in Hagia Sophia at which the union was read. The event caused intense discord, and many refused to take part in services in which the pope was commemorated. // The union did not bring the hoped-for military help and was not substantially applied. Constantinople fell on 29 May 1453. The episode shows the dilemma of the last Byzantines between faith and political survival, and historians continue to discuss it.

analysis|12-12|2008|Πεθαίνει ο Τάσσος Παπαδόπουλος|Tassos Papadopoulos dies|Tassos Papadopoulos was a lawyer and politician who from a young age took part in the EOKA struggle and then in the political life of Cyprus. He served as minister under President Makarios and represented the Greek Cypriot side in negotiations on the Cyprus issue. In 2003 he was elected President of the Republic of Cyprus. // His presidency was marked by the referendum of 2004 on the Annan plan, in which he himself called on Greek Cypriots to reject it. On 1 May 2004 Cyprus joined the European Union. He was not re-elected in 2008 and was defeated in the first round by Demetris Christofias. // He died in Nicosia in December 2008, at the age of 74. His politics still divide Cypriots: some believe he defended the rights of the community, others that a chance for a solution was lost. In this context his personality remains a point of reference in Cypriot politics.

analysis|12-13|1803|Το ολοκαύτωμα στο Κούγκι|The holocaust at Kougi|The Souliotes were a Christian community in Epirus that resisted Ali Pasha of Ioannina for decades. After a siege and hunger, in 1803 the Souliotes were forced to agree to surrender and to abandon their villages, but Ali Pasha did not always keep the agreements and attacked the groups that were leaving. // At Kougi, one of the Souliote strongholds, the monk Samouil, together with a few more defenders, stayed behind to cover the others. When Ali's forces approached, he blew up the powder store, killing himself, his companions and many attackers. // The act became a symbol of resistance and sacrifice and inspired the tradition of the holocaust, as later at Arkadi.
